items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves a free meal to all visitors

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice, originated by Guru Nanak, institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru) who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him
A meal restricted to initiated Khalsa Sikhs

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level to eat — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — recently in Ukraine, Turkey, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. The simple physical act of sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.

items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India
The Khalsa (the 'pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and gender
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surname Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women — symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers that emerged from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.

items.title: Judaism centres on covenant — a binding agreement with God
items.claim: What is the relationship between the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants in Judaism?

options.text: The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17, sealed by circumcision) promises land and descendants; the Mosaic covenant (Exodus 19-24, at Sinai) gives the Torah law — both remain binding on Jews
There is only one covenant — at Sinai
Covenants applied only to ancient Israelites, not modern Jews

items.reveal:
Brit milah (covenant of circumcision) is performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth, marking the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13). The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot (commandments) of the Torah law.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) — applying to all humanity — is also recognised. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot binding specifically on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not a vague concept of relationship. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.
